A postmortem is an examination or analysis that happens after something has ended — most often after a death, or after an event has concluded. The key idea is: it always happens after the fact, looking backward to understand something more fully.

The word has two main lives — one in medicine, and one in everyday language.

In medicine, a postmortem (also called an autopsy) is a thorough, systematic examination of a dead body carried out by a doctor — specifically a type of specialist called a pathologist — to answer questions that couldn't be answered while the person was alive.

What is the doctor actually trying to find out?

The central question is almost always: "Why did this person die?"

But it can go deeper than that:

  • The cause of death — What biological event killed them? (e.g., a heart attack, a brain bleed, organ failure, poisoning)
  • The manner of death — Was it natural, accidental, a suicide, or a homicide?
  • The time of death — How long ago did the person die?
  • The progression of disease — If someone was sick, how far had the disease spread? Did it behave the way doctors expected?
  • Whether a treatment worked — In some cases, doctors want to know if a surgery or medication actually had the intended effect.

Who orders a postmortem?

  • A coroner or medical examiner (a legal official) orders one when a death is sudden, suspicious, unexplained, or violent — such as in a murder case, a road accident, or when someone dies alone and their body is found later.
  • A hospital might request one (with the family's permission) when a patient dies in ways that raise medical questions — for example, when doctors want to learn from a puzzling case.
  • A family can sometimes request one if they are unsatisfied with the given cause of death or want closure.

What actually happens during a medical postmortem?

The process is methodical and careful:

  1. The pathologist examines the outside of the body — noting injuries, marks, skin color, and other external signs.
  2. They open the body and examine internal organs one by one — the heart, lungs, liver, brain, kidneys, and so on — looking for damage, disease, abnormalities, or signs of trauma.
  3. They may take tissue samples and send them to a laboratory for microscopic analysis.
  4. They may also run toxicology tests — testing blood or urine for the presence of drugs, alcohol, or poisons.
  5. Finally, the pathologist writes a postmortem report, which is an official document detailing all findings and stating the official cause of death.

This report can be critically important in criminal trials, insurance claims, medical research, and helping families find answers.

Outside of medicine, the word postmortem is used very widely in everyday life to describe any serious, structured review that takes place after an event — usually one that went badly or ended unexpectedly.

The logic is borrowed directly from medicine: just as a pathologist examines a body to understand why it died, people "examine" a failed or completed event to understand why it unfolded the way it did.

Where you'll hear this used:

In business and project management:
After a project fails, is delayed, or ends — whether successfully or not — a team holds a postmortem meeting. They go through what happened step by step, asking:

  • What went wrong?
  • What went right?
  • What should we do differently next time?

This is extremely common in tech companies, where it's sometimes also called a "retrospective" or "lessons learned" session.

In politics and journalism:
After an election, especially a surprising or devastating loss, political analysts conduct a postmortem of the campaign. They analyze every decision — the messaging, the strategy, the resources — to explain the outcome.

In sports:
After a team suffers a shocking defeat, coaches and commentators perform a postmortem of the game — reviewing tactics, player decisions, and turning points.

In everyday conversation:
If you and your friends planned a party that went terribly, and then sat down the next day to discuss everything that went wrong so you never repeat the same mistakes — that casual conversation is, in spirit, a postmortem.

Whether it's medical or figurative, every postmortem shares these traits:

  1. It is backward-looking. It examines something that has already happened or already ended. You cannot do a postmortem on something that is still ongoing.
  2. It is analytical. It's not just talking about what happened — it's carefully digging into what happened to understand it at a deeper level.
  3. It seeks a specific kind of truth. In medicine: the cause of death. In general use: the cause of failure (or the reasons for an unexpected outcome).
  4. It has a purpose beyond the past. The insights gained from a postmortem are meant to inform the future — whether that's justice in a court of law, better medical knowledge, or smarter decisions next time.

• The word carries a serious tone. When someone says "let's do a postmortem," they are signaling that something significant happened and deserves careful attention — not a casual chat.
  • In the figurative sense, a postmortem is usually associated with negative events (failures, losses, disasters), though it can occasionally be used after any significant event to extract lessons.
  • A postmortem is not a blame session. Its purpose is understanding, not punishing. In professional settings especially, a good postmortem focuses on systems and decisions, not on attacking individuals.
  • The plural is simply postmortems.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
A postmortem is a careful, after-the-fact examination — of a dead body in medicine, or of a failed/concluded event in general life — conducted to understand why things turned out the way they did.
